entry.title: Reimplementing BPE from the survey: do the three code listings agree, and is the fast one really faster?

link.title: Reimplementing BPE from the survey: do the three code listings agree, and is the fast one really faster?

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

Section 3.1 (Byte-pair encoding) of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP. The survey prints three short Python listings:

  • Code 3.1: BPE training. Start from characters, and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair.
  • Code 3.2: BPE inference, iterative version. Try every merge in the list, in order.
  • Code 3.3: BPE inference, priority version. Find the earliest merge that applies, apply it, repeat.

The survey makes several claims about them that I could check:

  1. Code 3.3 is “equivalent to” Code 3.2 (caption of Code 3.3).
  2. Code 3.2 wastes computation, and the waste grows with the merge list (Section 3.1.2).
  3. Merging frequent pairs “tends to surface linguistically meaningful units such as morphemes” (start of Section 3.1).

The other reimplementation of this paper (MaxMatch vs. PathPiece, Section 3.6) is about general inference algorithms. This post is about the BPE trainer and its two decoders. The experiments below are mine, not results from the survey.

The code

I typed the three listings exactly as printed (the PDF lost the indentation of two lines, which I restored) and ran them as they are. As an independent check, I wrote a second implementation that does not copy their loops: it counts each distinct word once (the “pretoken-to-count dictionary” optimization that the survey mentions but does not show) and merges only in words that contain the pair.

# Code 3.1 core: the whole trainer is this loop
while len(vocab) < target_vocabulary_size:
    pair_counts = collections.Counter(
        (a, b) for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus for a, b in zip(pretoken, pretoken[1:]))
    if len(pair_counts) == 0: break
    max_pair = max(pair_counts, key=pair_counts.get)   # ties: first pair seen
    merges.append(max_pair)
    vocab.append(max_pair[0] + max_pair[1])
    for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus:
        apply_merge(pretoken, max_pair)

Full code: survey_bpe.py (the survey’s listings), fast_bpe.py (my independent version), run_experiments.py, make_figure.py, and the raw numbers in results.json. It uses only the Python standard library, plus Matplotlib for the figure.

Data. Training: Pride and Prejudice (718,465 characters, 148,283 words, 8,517 distinct). Testing, never seen in training: Frankenstein (418,285 characters, 84,702 words, 7,831 distinct). Both are plain-text Project Gutenberg ebooks (numbers 1342 and 84). The alphabet has 90 characters.

Results

1. The listings run, and the docstring is right

pretokenize("Hello, world!") returns exactly the list in the survey’s docstring. Training 1,000 merges on the novel gives a sensible start: ` t, he, a, in, w, s, re, o, ha, the, er, ou, en`, … (the leading space belongs to the next word, because of the survey’s pretokenizer).

2. Cross-check: the independent trainer gives the same 1,000 merges

My independent implementation produced exactly the same merge list, in the same order (identical, 1,000 of 1,000). The survey’s Code 3.1 took 46 seconds for these 1,000 merges, and my version 5 seconds. That is the “pretoken-to-count dictionary” speed-up in practice (about 9 times).

Note: this match holds because I copied the survey’s tie-breaking rule (the first pair seen wins a tie). The survey does not say that this rule matters, but a different tie-break gives a different tokenizer.

3. Claim 1: Code 3.3 equals Code 3.2. Confirmed, with no exception

With the 1,000-merge list I tokenized all 7,831 distinct words of the held-out novel, and also about 5,000 random strings over a tiny alphabet, which are meant to hit unusual merge chains. Code 3.2, Code 3.3 and my independent encoder gave identical output on every single input (0 differences). This is a test, not a proof, but it covers far more than hand examples.

4. Claim 2: the iterative decoder wastes work, and the waste grows with the merge list. Confirmed

I timed both decoders on 3,000 words while making the merge list longer:

Merges in the list Code 3.2 (iterative) Code 3.3 (priority) Ratio
100 0.033 s 0.007 s 5×
500 0.132 s 0.010 s 14×
1,000 0.227 s 0.010 s 23×
2,000 0.393 s 0.011 s 37×
4,000 0.684 s 0.011 s 61×

Code 3.2’s time grows with the length of the merge list, because each word is checked against every merge. Code 3.3 stays almost flat, because it only looks at merges that really appear in the word. The survey notes that modern tokenizers have hundreds of thousands of merges, which is why this matters.

5. Claim 3: “surfaces morphemes”. Partly

Characters per token on the held-out novel grow from 1.00 (no merges) to 1.54 (50 merges), 2.50 (500), 2.86 (1,000) and 3.67 (4,000 merges), as the right panel shows. For the claim about morphemes:

  • Supported: common endings become tokens early. er is merge number 11, ed 20, ing 25, ly 49. Whole frequent words come soon too: the first four whole words formed are ` the, and, her and was`.
  • Not supported for rarer words. With 4,000 merges, The unbelievably unfriendly creatures were running quickly. becomes T | he | ␣un | b | e | lie | v | ably | ␣unf | ri | end | ly | ␣creat | ures | ␣were | ␣running | ␣quick | ly | . (␣ marks the space that belongs to the next word). unfriendly is split as unf | ri | end | ly, which cuts across its morphemes (un-friend-ly), and unbelievably ends in ably rather than -ly. Frequency finds the units that are frequent in this book, which are often but not always morphemes.

What I learned

  • Trust but check the listing. The three printed listings agree with each other, and with an independent implementation. The thing that was not obvious is that the tie-breaking rule is part of the algorithm.
  • “Equivalent” is easy to test. A few lines of code that compare two decoders over thousands of inputs are worth more than the sentence “equivalent” in a caption. Here the claim holds.
  • The decoder gap is large and grows with the vocabulary. Even with a merge list of only 4,000 (the survey says modern tokenizers have hundreds of thousands), the iterative decoder was already 61 times slower.
  • Caveats. The timings are one run on one laptop, on 3,000 words, so only the trend and the order of magnitude matter. I used English novels only; the survey’s points about other languages would need other text. I did not compare with a production library such as Hugging Face tokenizers or tiktoken, which use a different pretokenizer and tie-break rules.
entry.summary: Running Codes 3.1 to 3.3 of the tokenization survey on two novels, cross-checking them with an independent implementation, and testing the survey's claims about equivalence, wasted computation and morphemes.

entry.title: Critique: Parameter-efficient, but is it compute-efficient?

link.title: Critique: Parameter-efficient, but is it compute-efficient?

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper (Geiping et al., 2025) proposes a language model whose middle block is applied repeatedly in latent space before producing the next token. The main claims are:

  1. Recurrent depth can be trained at scale. Using a shared recurrent block, randomly sampled iteration counts, and truncated backpropagation, the authors train a 3.5B parameter model on approximately 800B tokens.
  2. More iterations at test time improve performance, especially on reasoning tasks such as GSM8K and ARC-Challenge, reaching a computation load equivalent to much larger models.
  3. No special Chain-of-Thought training data is required. The model learns to use additional computation through standard next-token prediction, without explicitly supervised reasoning traces.
  4. The architecture naturally supports additional inference techniques, including adaptive exits, KV-cache sharing, and potentially self-speculative decoding.
  5. Structured dynamics emerge in latent space, including convergence patterns, orbits, and directional drifts, which the authors suggest may be related to internal reasoning mechanisms.

Strengths

  • A convincing demonstration at scale. The authors show that a recurrent-depth language model can be trained with billions of parameters and hundreds of billions of tokens. Increasing test-time recurrence substantially improves performance. On GSM8K CoT, the model achieves 42.08% flexible accuracy at 32 iterations (Table 2), compared with almost no success at a single iteration.
  • No explicit CoT supervision is required. The model learns to benefit from additional computation during regular language-model training, without requiring labeled intermediate reasoning steps.
  • Interesting inference capabilities. The experiments suggest that adaptive computation and KV-cache sharing can be applied without additional training. The possibility of self-speculative decoding is also interesting, although its practical speedup is not demonstrated.
  • Transparency and reproducibility. The authors release their model, code, and training data. They also discuss failed training runs and the stability problems they encountered (Figure 5), which provides useful information for future research.

Weaknesses

1. Parameters are matched, but compute is not

The fixed-depth baseline in Table 4 uses the same basic architecture with only one pass through the recurrent block and is trained on the same 180B tokens. However, at 32 iterations, the recurrent model has an effective depth of:

\[2 + 4 \cdot 32 + 2 = 132\]

compared with only 8 layers for the baseline. Therefore, the recurrent model uses substantially more training computation per token.

The authors acknowledge this issue, noting that their model consumes pretraining FLOPs comparable to a much larger standard Transformer. For example, a rough parameter-token estimate suggests a training compute budget comparable to, or potentially greater than, that of some larger models used in the comparisons. This is not an exact FLOP comparison, but it illustrates why parameter count alone can be misleading.

Interestingly, Table 4 also shows that at a single recurrence, where inference costs are more comparable, the recurrent model performs worse than the fixed-depth baseline (34.01% vs. 46.42% on ARC-E at 180B tokens). However, this comparison is also limited because the recurrent model was mainly trained with much greater depth.

I think the results demonstrate parameter efficiency, but do not establish compute efficiency. This does not invalidate the contribution, since reducing parameter count can be valuable for memory and communication costs. However, the distinction should be clearer.

A related limitation is the lack of a direct comparison with Chain-of-Thought at the same inference compute budget. The paper presents latent reasoning as an alternative or complement to verbalized reasoning, but does not establish when additional recurrent iterations are preferable to generating more reasoning tokens.

2. The latent-space analysis shows structure, not necessarily reasoning

Section 7 presents interesting patterns in the hidden-state trajectories, including orbits, convergence, and directional drifts. The authors suggest these might represent internal computational mechanisms.

However, these conclusions are based mainly on qualitative visualizations of selected tokens, projected onto a small number of PCA directions.

For example, the orbit observed for the token “3” in Figure 12 might be related to arithmetic processing, but the visualization alone does not establish that the model is actually performing an arithmetic operation through this trajectory.

The authors are generally careful in their wording, using expressions such as “could serve” and “suggests”. Nevertheless, the connection between these geometric patterns and reasoning remains speculative.

A reimplementation by another student in this course also illustrates how difficult it is to interpret these trajectories. Different contexts produce different patterns of convergence, but these observations do not directly establish what computations are taking place.

Moreover, the path-independence experiments investigate the effect of changing the initial state, rather than testing whether specific trajectories causally contribute to the final prediction.

How it could have been improved

  • FLOP-matched baselines. Compare the recurrent model with standard Transformers trained under the same total compute budget, using larger models, more training tokens, or greater fixed depth.
  • Recurrence vs. Chain-of-Thought. Compare additional recurrent iterations against longer CoT generation or multiple sampled solutions under the same inference FLOP budget.
  • More systematic trajectory analysis. Measure how frequently different patterns occur across tasks and tokens, and whether they correlate with correct predictions. For example, compare numerical tokens in arithmetic problems with identical tokens in ordinary text.
  • Causal interventions. Modify or suppress particular directions in latent space during recurrence and measure their effect on performance. This could provide stronger evidence that the observed trajectories are functionally important rather than simply correlated with the task.

Verdict

Accept.

I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution by demonstrating that recurrent-depth language models can be trained at scale and can benefit substantially from additional test-time computation. The training methodology, open release, and experimental results make it a valuable proof of concept.

However, the comparisons with larger models should be interpreted primarily in terms of parameter efficiency rather than compute efficiency. Similarly, the latent-space analysis should be viewed as exploratory rather than direct evidence of specific reasoning mechanisms.

Is the direction worth pursuing? Yes. I think recurrent depth is a promising approach to test-time computation, especially if future work can establish its advantages under equal compute budgets and provide stronger evidence about the computations performed in latent space.
entry.summary: A solid proof of concept at scale, but the comparisons do not control for compute, and the latent-space figures show structure rather than reasoning.

entry.title: Reimplementing Greedy vs. Shortest-Path Tokenization
entry.content:
What I reimplemented

I focused on Section 3.6 of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP, specifically Figure 3.2 and Example 3.3 (p. 25). The survey contrasts MaxMatch, which greedily takes the longest vocabulary prefix from left to right, with PathPiece, which finds a segmentation that uses the fewest tokens (a shortest path through a segmentation lattice).

I implemented both inference algorithms from scratch in Python, without training a tokenizer or running a language model. First, I reproduced the survey’s concrete example using its exact input and vocabulary. Then I extended the comparison to a small, exhaustive synthetic benchmark to measure how often MaxMatch uses more tokens than PathPiece.

The extension is my own experiment, not a reported result from the survey.

The code

The central difference is the local greedy choice versus the globally optimal dynamic-programming recurrence:

def maxmatch(text, vocabulary):
    vocab = set(vocabulary)
    output = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(text):
        # Take the longest valid token starting at position i.
        matches = [t for t in vocab if text.startswith(t, i)]
        if not matches:
            raise ValueError("No valid segmentation")
        token = max(matches, key=len)
        output.append(token)
        i += len(token)
    return output


def pathpiece(text, vocabulary):
    vocab = set(vocabulary)
    n = len(text)
    dp = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
    choice = [None] * (n + 1)
    dp[n] = 0

    # dp[i] = minimum tokens required to segment text[i:].
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for token in sorted(vocab, key=lambda t: (-len(t), t)):
            if text.startswith(token, i):
                candidate = 1 + dp[i + len(token)]
                if candidate < dp[i]:
                    dp[i] = candidate
                    choice[i] = token

    if dp[0] == float("inf"):
        raise ValueError("No valid segmentation")
    output = []
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        output.append(choice[i])
        i += len(choice[i])
    return output

The full script includes input validation, automated assertions, exhaustive enumeration, a results CSV, and plotting. It uses only standard Python plus Matplotlib for the figure.

Full code: tokenization_experiment.py

Results

1. Reproducing the survey’s example

Using the paper’s input abcdefg and vocabulary {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, abc, abcd, bcdef, defg}, the implementation produced:

Method Segmentation Token count
MaxMatch abcd | e | f | g 4
PathPiece abc | defg 2

This exactly matches Figure 3.2 and Example 3.3 in the survey. MaxMatch commits to abcd, leaving three single-character tokens; PathPiece instead chooses abc | defg, requiring only two tokens.

2. New synthetic experiment (not reported in the survey)

To measure how often the greedy method is suboptimal, I fixed the synthetic vocabulary

{a, b, aa, aaa, aaaa, ab, aba, abab, abb, baab, bab, baba, bbab, bbbb}

and enumerated all 2,046 binary strings of lengths 1 through 10. Both algorithms use exactly the same fixed vocabulary, which includes the single characters to ensure every input can be segmented.

The metric is the fraction of strings for which

len(MaxMatch(s)) > len(PathPiece(s)).

String length Strings tested Greedy suboptimal Failure rate
4 16 2 12.50%
6 64 14 21.88%
8 256 57 22.27%
10 1,024 279 27.25%
All lengths 1–10 2,046 507 24.78%

The plot and numerical results are generated by the script. These measurements are not numbers from the survey and should not be interpreted as real-world failure rates for production tokenizers. They depend on the synthetic vocabulary and the input distribution. Because PathPiece explicitly minimizes token count, its count cannot be worse than MaxMatch’s for the same vocabulary.

What I learned

A locally reasonable segmentation choice does not necessarily optimize the complete sequence. In the paper’s example, taking the longest prefix forces MaxMatch into a worse segmentation, whereas dynamic programming considers how today’s choice affects the remaining suffix.

The exhaustive comparison gave a simple way to quantify this phenomenon, not just demonstrate one counterexample. It also highlighted an important distinction: minimum token count is a specific objective, not a guarantee of better downstream language-model quality. Real tokenizers may prioritize other properties, and the survey notes that inference algorithms can have different objectives.
entry.summary: Reproducing the survey's MaxMatch vs. PathPiece example and measuring when greedy segmentation is suboptimal on 2,046 synthetic strings.

entry.title: Learning about Information Bottleneck
entry.content:
What makes a latent representation good?

Can we tell whether a model’s latent representation is good? The information bottleneck gives us a way to ask a more precise question. How much of the input does the representation need to retain to predict a particular target?

The information bottleneck

In 1999, Naftali Tishby, Fernando C. Pereira, and William Bialek proposed a way to think about representations using information theory and rate–distortion theory. Their idea was to compress an input while preserving as much information as possible about a target. A representation can discard details that matter for one task and still be excellent for another.

Let $X$ be the input, $Z$ its compressed representation, and $Y$ the target. The information bottleneck objective is $\min_{p(z\mid x)}\bigl[I(X;Z)-\beta I(Z;Y)\bigr]$. Here, $I(X;Z)$ measures how much information $Z$ retains about the input, and $I(Z;Y)$ measures how much knowing $Z$ reduces uncertainty about the target. A larger $\beta$ gives more weight to preserving target information. In language modeling, a natural choice is to take $X$ as the preceding context and $Y$ as the next token.

Reading the information plane

Plot input information $I(X;Z)$ on the horizontal axis and target information $I(Z;Y)$ on the vertical axis. For a fixed joint distribution of inputs and targets, the information bottleneck frontier gives the most target information any encoding can retain at a given input-information budget. Points above it are unattainable. A point below it leaves room to retain more target information at the same budget.

An illustrative frontier. The figure uses $B$ for the representation denoted by $Z$ in the text.

What happens during LLM training?

Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby reported two phases in early neural-network experiments. During fitting, representations became more informative about the target. During compression, they shed input information while retaining much of their predictive information. Whether this pattern generalizes across architectures and training setups remains an empirical question.

In Learning is Forgetting, Henry Conklin and colleagues applied a soft entropy estimator to LLM activations. The estimator softly assigns normalized activation vectors to reference directions, then uses the resulting distribution to estimate entropy. This makes it practical to track how much information the representations carry about selected input and output features across training checkpoints.

In OLMo 2 7B, the authors observed an initial expansion in the estimated input and target information, followed by a phase in which input information fell and the ratio $I(Z;Y)/I(X;Z)$ rose. The dashed diagonal in their plot represents the data-processing upper bound $I(Z;Y)\leq I(X;Z)$ in the idealized setting where $Z$ is encoded from $X$. The true frontier depends on the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ and can lie below that diagonal. The trajectory shows how the estimated trade-off changed during training under the paper’s measurement setup.

Figure 1 from Conklin et al. (2026).

What changes during reasoning?

The reason I think this relates to looped transformers is that the information bottleneck framework suggests a way to think about the reasoning process. The information plane can help us understand how the model’s representation changes as it reasons. Instead of comparing training checkpoints, we could hold the model fixed and compare successive reasoning steps. In text chain-of-thought, the next-token target changes as the model writes, and different stretches of text can serve different subtasks. A looped transformer can update its latent state several times before emitting a token. Which intermediate quantities become accessible during those updates is an empirical question.

References

  • Tishby, Pereira, and Bialek. The Information Bottleneck Method. 1999 conference paper, posted to arXiv in 2000.
  • Tishby and Zaslavsky. Deep Learning and the Information Bottleneck Principle. 2015.
  • Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby. Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information. 2017.
  • Conklin et al. Learning is Forgetting: LLM Training As Lossy Compression. 2026.
entry.summary: How can we measure the usefulness of latent representations?

entry.title: Reproducing the exit rule and the latent trajectories on Huginn-0125

link.title: Reproducing the exit rule and the latent trajectories on Huginn-0125

entry.content:
What was reimplemented

The authors released the trained model, Huginn-0125. Two parts of the paper were reproduced on it. The first is the adaptive exit rule from Section 6.1, which stops the recurrence for a token once the next-token distribution has stopped changing between consecutive trips. The second is the latent trajectory analysis from Section 7, where the hidden state of a token is plotted trip by trip in its two leading principal directions. Both were run on a single input: Tom has 12 apples and buys 29 more. How many apples does he have now?

Setup

The model was run on a MacBook with an Apple M4 chip and 24 GB of memory. In bfloat16 it occupies about 8 GB. Each generated token took about 12 seconds at 64 trips, and the two prompts used in this post took under ten minutes in total.

The code

The model exposes three methods that allow the recurrence to be driven step by step. embed_inputs runs the embedding and the prelude once and returns the vector \(e\) for every position. iterate_one_step runs one trip through the core block. predict_from_latents applies the coda and the unembedding to a state and returns the logits. The loop below runs 64 trips and, after each one, computes the next-token distribution at every position and the KL divergence from the distribution one trip earlier, following the authors’ KL exit criterion.

emb, block_idx = model.embed_inputs(ids)          # prelude output e, computed once
x = model.initialize_state(emb)                    # random starting state s_0
prev = torch.full((S, V), -math.log(V))            # uniform distribution for the first comparison
for step in range(64):
    x, block_idx, _ = model.iterate_one_step(emb, x, block_idx=block_idx, current_step=step)
    lp = torch.log_softmax(model.predict_from_latents(x).logits[0].float(), -1)
    kl = (prev.exp() * (prev - lp)).sum(-1)        # one value per position
    # the first trip with kl < 5e-4 is the exit trip of that position; x is stored for the trajectory plots
    prev = lp

Generation runs this loop once per new token on the full sequence, without a KV cache. The next token is the most likely token at the last position at that position’s exit trip. It is appended and the loop runs again. Decoding is greedy.

The full code is here.

Results

The model’s answer is Tom now has 12 + 29 = 41 apples. The fourteen generated tokens exit between trip 7 and trip 28, with a mean of 14.6. The answer therefore used 205 trips through the core block, compared with 448 for a fixed budget of 32 trips per token.

Within the question, the exit trips are not uniform. The words How, many and does exit after 9 to 12 trips. The digits of 12 and 29 take 23 to 30 trips, and the digit 2 of 12 does not reach the threshold within 64 trips. In the answer, the first digit of 12 takes 28 trips and the plus sign 20, while apples takes 7.

Output at each trip

For every answer position, the token that the coda would output after each trip was recorded. The figure shows these tokens for trips 1 to 32. Several positions change in the first ten trips. The answer digit is 1, 2, 5 and 3 on trips 1 to 5 and 4 from trip 6 onward. The position of the plus sign alternates between + and apples until trip 11. The position of now passes through is, has, originally and initially before trip 11. No position changes after trip 11, up to trip 64.

The exit rule stopped every position after its last change, so the generated answer is identical to the one obtained with 64 trips. On this input the rule is conservative: all positions had settled by trip 11, and most exits came later.

Latent trajectories

The figure below shows the hidden state of each token in the question on trips 33 to 64, projected onto the two leading principal directions of that token’s own trajectory over those trips. Trips 1 to 32 are excluded because the state moves much more in the first trips than afterwards, and including them would compress the later trips into a single point.

In this window, the state of most tokens moves along a closed or spiral path rather than converging to a point. The step length per trip is roughly constant from trip 25 onward, at about 1/300 of the first step. The tokens that exited earliest show the most regular loops. The paper reports orbits for selected tokens in Figure 10; on this input the same behaviour appears for most of the sentence.

Discussion

The number of trips a token uses before the exit rule fires varies between 7 and 35 within one short input, and the longest counts occur on the digits and on the tokens where the answer’s format is decided. The hidden state continues to move after the output has stopped changing, which is consistent with the authors’ choice of a criterion on the output distribution rather than on the state.

These results come from one prompt, one random initial state and greedy decoding. They illustrate the mechanisms described in the paper but do not measure the model’s accuracy or the savings from adaptive exit in general.
entry.summary: Per-token exit trips, what the answer would be if the loop stopped early, and the latent trajectories of every token, measured on the released model.

entry.title: literature review of recurrent depth latent reasoning

link.title: literature review of recurrent depth latent reasoning

entry.content:
The authors’ path

The first and last authors of Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach are Jonas Geiping and Tom Goldstein. Their previous research provides two particularly relevant foundations for this paper: making language models more computationally efficient, and enabling neural networks to solve harder problems by performing more computation.

Jonas Geiping: Making language models more efficient

Jonas Geiping is a researcher at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems. His research focuses on the efficiency, safety, and reliability of modern machine learning systems, particularly large language models.

One of his most relevant earlier works is Cramming: Training a Language Model on a Single GPU in One Day (ICML 2023), co-authored with Tom Goldstein.

Rather than asking how much performance could be gained by increasing computational resources, they explored how much could be achieved under strict computational constraints. By optimizing the training pipeline, they demonstrated that a BERT-like language model could achieve competitive performance after just 24 hours of training on a single GPU.

The connection to the current paper is clear: both studies challenge the assumption that improving language models necessarily requires increasing their parameter count. While Cramming investigated how to use a limited training budget efficiently, the recurrent-depth paper explores how to use additional computation at inference time without increasing the number of model parameters.

Tom Goldstein: From optimization to recurrent reasoning

Tom Goldstein is a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Maryland and Director of the Maryland Center for Machine Learning. His research combines optimization, machine learning, and efficient computing.

The recurrent-depth paper builds especially closely on his earlier research into what his group calls “deep thinking” networks.

In The Uncanny Similarity of Recurrence and Depth (2021), Goldstein and his collaborators showed that recurrent neural networks could reproduce some of the benefits of deeper feedforward networks by repeatedly applying the same layers.

This idea was extended in Can You Learn an Algorithm? Generalizing from Easy to Hard Problems with Recurrent Networks (NeurIPS 2021). The researchers demonstrated that recurrent networks trained on relatively simple reasoning problems, such as small mazes, could generalize to harder instances by performing additional iterations at inference time.

These results established a central motivation for the current paper: a model’s computational depth does not have to be fixed at training time. Instead, the model can reuse learned operations for as long as a problem requires.

How their research connects to this paper

The recurrent-depth paper can be viewed as a convergence of these two research directions:

  • From Geiping and Goldstein’s Cramming: Efficient model design and careful use of computational resources can provide alternatives to simply increasing model size.
  • From Goldstein’s earlier deep-thinking research: Recurrent computation enables models to increase their effective depth and potentially solve harder problems without introducing additional parameters.

The current work combines these ideas at the scale of modern language modeling. The authors train a 3.5-billion-parameter Transformer with a recurrent block that can be executed repeatedly at inference time, allowing the model to perform additional reasoning internally rather than generating longer chains of thought.

The important progression is from demonstrating recurrence on relatively controlled reasoning tasks to testing whether the same principle can work in a large-scale, pretrained language model.

This makes the paper more than an isolated architectural experiment. It represents a continuation of the authors’ broader investigation into how neural networks can use computation more effectively, both during training and at inference time.

The bigger picture

The authors’ research trajectory suggests an alternative perspective on scaling language models. Instead of treating parameter count and training data as the primary ways to improve performance, their work investigates whether the organization and allocation of computation can be equally important.

The recurrent-depth paper is an important step in this direction, although it leaves open whether latent recurrence can match the reasoning capabilities and efficiency of leading models that rely on explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

The main takeaway: This paper connects two established research threads from its authors: efficient language-model training and recurrent neural computation. Its novelty lies in bringing these ideas together to demonstrate test-time reasoning through increased depth rather than increased token generation.
entry.summary: How Jonas Geiping and Tom Goldstein's earlier work on efficient language models and recurrent computation converged in a new approach to test-time scaling.

entry.title: Before you read MSAR: the three ideas it builds on

link.title: Before you read MSAR: the three ideas it builds on

entry.content:
Our reading group spent this week on “Multi-Stream Attention Residuals” (Qin et al., 2026), which proposes a new way to connect the layers of a Transformer and reports solid gains on 18B and 28B parameter models.

The paper builds on three earlier ideas and assumes you already know them. This post walks through those ideas in order, with the problem each one leaves open, and shows how the last of those problems leads directly to MSAR. If the background is familiar, skip to the final section.

The question

A token passes through the layers of a Transformer one by one, and each layer changes it a little. So every architecture has to decide: how does a layer draw on the layers below it? The three ideas below are three answers.

Answer 1 · Residual connections: add everything

This is the standard connection. Each layer adds its output to a running sum, and the next layer reads that sum. It is simple and stable, and it works. The cost is that every output lands in the same vector with the same weight. As the network gets deeper, the contribution of early layers is diluted, and nothing downstream can recover it on its own.

Answer 2 · Hyper-Connections: several streams in parallel

Hyper-Connections replace the single residual stream with several streams that run through the whole network, mixed at every layer by learned matrices. Information no longer has to collapse into one sum. mHC from DeepSeek, which the paper refers to often, is a variant that constrains the mixing matrices to keep training stable.

The limitation is that the mixing is learned once and then frozen. Every token, on every input, gets the same mix. But which layer holds the useful information varies from token to token: for one token it is layer 2, for the next it is layer 7. A fixed mix cannot track that. Running several streams also multiplies memory.

Answer 3 · Attention Residuals: let the input decide

Attention Residuals replace the sum with attention over the outputs of the earlier layers. It is the familiar mechanism, applied along the depth axis rather than the sequence axis. The twist is that there are no Q, K or V projections. Each layer has a single learned query vector, and those earlier outputs serve as both keys and values. The method adds almost no parameters, yet the weights now depend on the input: one token can draw mostly on layer 2 while its neighbour draws on layer 7.

The three answers. Arrow width shows how much the top layer takes from each earlier layer. Only in the third case does the pattern change from token to token.

The problem that remains: a single head

Attention over the sequence uses several heads, each with its own view of the sentence. What makes them different is either separate projection matrices or separate slices of the vector. Attention Residuals has neither option: there are no matrices, and slicing the vector degrades the selection. Run four heads and they all see the same outputs, so they end up nearly identical. This is the point where MSAR begins.

What MSAR adds

MSAR gives each head a different view without adding matrices or slicing the vector. Before a head selects among layers, each output is passed through a causal convolution along the sequence, blending in a few of the preceding tokens, and each head uses a different window size. The four heads therefore see four slightly different views of the same column and make different selections. How the heads are fused, and why this costs no extra memory, is covered in the method section, which reads easily once this background is in place.

Left: four heads without the convolution see identical inputs. Right: each head gets its own window, and so its own selection.

One reading tip: the paper calls this a “depth-wise” convolution, but it runs over tokens, not over layers. The attention is along depth; the convolution is along the sequence.

In short

There are three ways to connect layers, and what separates them is whether the weights are fixed or computed from the input. Attention Residuals is the dynamic one, but without projection matrices it is limited to a single head. MSAR gives each head a different window over the sequence, and that is the whole idea. With these three pieces in place, the paper is a straightforward read.

Posted at: LinkedIn · X
entry.summary: A short guide to the background the paper assumes: residual connections, Hyper-Connections and Attention Residuals, and the problem that leads to MSAR.

entry.title: Copyediting Section 7 of Recurrent Depth
entry.content:
What I changed and why

Section 7 is intriguing because it is where the paper looks directly at what the recurrence does to a token’s latent state as the model iterates. With that being said, the section does not separate what the authors observed from what they infer, and several claims extend beyond the figures: the title attributes the patterns to scale although no smaller model is shown, and the text and captions disagree on how widely orbits occur and what sliders are for. I introduced the three patterns up front, stated the evidence base once, moved the interpretations to a closing paragraph and removed claims the figures do not support, reducing the section from 568 to under 400 words.

Before and after

Before

Finally, what is the model doing while recurring in latent space? To understand this question better, we analyze the trajectories { 𝐬 i } i = 1 r of the model on a few qualitative examples. We are especially interested in understanding what patterns emerge, simply by training this model at scale. In comparison to previous work, such as Bai et al. (2019), where the training objective directly encodes a prior that pushes trajectories to a fixed point, we only train with our truncated unrolling objective.

Figure 11 shows the norm distance ‖ 𝐬 i − 𝐬 ∗ ‖ between each 𝐬 i in a trajectory and an approximate limit point 𝐬 ∗ computed with 128 iterations. We show the sentence top to bottom and iterations from left to right. We clearly see that convergence behavior depends on context. We see that key parts of the question, and the start of the model response, are “deliberated” much more in latent space. The context dependence can also be seen in the different behavior among the three identical tokens representing each of the three dots. Also note that the distance to 𝐬 ∗ does not always decrease monotonically (e.g. for school); the model may also trace out complicated orbits in its latent trajectory while processing information, even though this is not represented explicitly in our training objective.

We look at trajectories for select tokens in more detail in Figure 12. We compute a PCA decomposition of latent trajectories over all tokens in a sequence, and then show several individual trajectories projected onto the first six PCA directions. See the appendix for more examples. Many tokens simply converge to a fixed point, such as the token in the top row. Yet, for harder questions, such as in the 2nd row5, the state of the token quickly falls into an orbit pattern in all three pairs of PCA directions. The use of multi-dimensional orbits like these could serve a similar purpose to periodic patterns sometimes observed in fixed-depth transformers trained for arithmetic tasks (Nanda et al., 2022), but we find these patterns extend far beyond arithmetic for our model. We often also observe the use of orbits on tokens such as “makes” (see Figure 16) or “thinks” that determine the structure of the response.

Aside from orbits, we also observe the model encoding particular key tokens as “sliders”, as seen in the middle of the bottom row in Figure 12 (which is the token “wrong”, from the same message as already shown in Figure 11). In these motions the trajectory noticeably drifts in a single direction, which the model could use to implement a mechanism to count how many iterations have occurred.

The emergence of structured trajectories in latent space gives us a glimpse into how the model performs its computations. Unlike the discrete sequential chain of reasoning seen in verbalized chain-of-thought approaches, we observe rich geometric patterns including orbits, convergent paths, and drifts - means to organize its computational process spatially. This suggests the model is independently learning to leverage the high-dimensional nature of its latent space to implement reasoning in new ways.

Path Independence. We verify that our models maintain path independence, in the sense of Anil et al. (2022), despite their complex, learned dynamics, which we discussed prior (see also the additional examples in Appendix Figure 22). When re-initializing from multiple starting states 𝐬 0 , the model moves in similar trajectories, exhibiting consistent behavior. The same orbital patterns, fixed points, or directional drifts emerge regardless of initialization.

After

What Patterns Emerge in Latent Space

What does the model compute while it iterates in latent space? We examine the trajectories \(\{\mathbf{s}_i\}_{i=1}^{r}\) of every token in a small set of hand-picked prompts, so the analysis in this section is qualitative. Unlike deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019), our training objective does not pull the state toward a fixed point, so any structure in these trajectories is learned by the model rather than imposed by the objective.

In these examples, each token’s state follows one of three patterns. Figure 12 shows selected trajectories projected onto the leading PCA directions of the prompt. Many tokens converge to a fixed point. Others enter an orbit and keep circling instead of converging. We observe orbits on numbers in math problems, such as the “3” in a GSM8k question about a three-egg omelette (see also Figure 16), and on some tokens that shape the response, such as “makes” and “thinks”, but not on trivia questions. A third group, which we call sliders, drifts steadily in one direction, for example the token “wrong” in an unsafe prompt.

Convergence speed depends on context, not only on the token itself. Figure 11 plots each token’s distance to \(\mathbf{s}^*\), its state after 128 iterations. The key words of the question and the first tokens of the response converge most slowly, and three identical dot tokens in the same prompt behave differently. For some tokens, such as “school”, the distance oscillates rather than decreasing monotonically.

These patterns do not depend on the initial state. Restarting the iteration from different random states \(\mathbf{s}_0\) yields the same fixed point, orbit or slide for each token (Appendix Figure 22), consistent with the path independence (Anil et al., 2022) that the random initialization is designed to promote (Section 3.1).

The function of these patterns remains speculative. Orbits on numbers may serve a role similar to the periodic representations found in transformers trained on arithmetic (Nanda et al., 2022). Sliders could act as a counter of elapsed iterations, or hold a concept the model is still processing. A handful of examples cannot distinguish between these possibilities, and we do not test either hypothesis here.

The general rule

Separate observation from interpretation. Report what the evidence shows first, and present any interpretation afterwards, explicitly marked as a hypothesis. A useful check is that deleting every interpretive sentence should still leave a complete and accurate description of the results.
entry.summary: Section 7 interleaves observation and speculation about the model's latent trajectories; this edit separates the two.

entry.title: A Scalable Recurrent Architecture - Rewritten for Easier Understanding

link.title: A Scalable Recurrent Architecture - Rewritten for Easier Understanding

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The main problem I had with the original text was that it had many equations without an in-depth explanation of each. Making it the readers responsibility to cross-reference with the figure.

As for the structure of the text, I personally would prefer having the motivation prior to the actual architecture. This helps understanding the reasons for such architecture choices and creates a more natural reading flow. Furthermore I try to include subtitles and lists whenever is possible to avoid large text blobs.

Before and after

Before

3.1. Macroscopic Design

The model is primarily structured around decoder-only transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017; Radford et al., 2019). However these blocks are structured into three functional groups, the prelude \(P\), which embeds the input data into a latent space using multiple transformer layers, then the core recurrent block \(R\), which is the central unit of recurrent computation modifying states \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\), and finally the coda \(C\), which un-embeds from latent space using several layers and also contains the prediction head of the model. The core block is set between the prelude and coda blocks, and by looping the core we can put an indefinite amount of verses in our song.

Given a number of recurrent iterations \(r\), and a sequence of input tokens \(\mathbf{x} \in V^{n}\) these groups are used in the following way to produce output probabilities \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times |V|}\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{e} &= P(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{s}_0 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_{n \cdot h}) \\ \mathbf{s}_i &= R(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{s}_{i-1}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, \dots, r\} \\ \mathbf{p} &= C(\mathbf{s}_r) \end{aligned} \]

where \(\sigma\) is some standard deviation for initializing the random state. This process is shown in Figure 2. Given an initial random state \(\mathbf{s}_0\), the model repeatedly applies the core block \(R\), which accepts the latent state \(\mathbf{s}_{i-1}\) and the embedded input \(\mathbf{e}\) and outputs a new latent state \(\mathbf{s}_i\). After finishing all iterations, the coda block processes the last state and produces the probabilities of the next token.

This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs \(\mathbf{e}\) in every step (Bansal et al., 2022) and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization, i.e. path independence (Anil et al., 2022).

Motivation for this Design. This recurrent design is the minimal setup required to learn stable iterative operators. A good example is gradient descent of a function \(E(x, y)\), where \(x\) may be the variable of interest and \(y\) the data. Gradient descent on this function starts from an initial random state, here \(x_0\), and repeatedly applies a simple operation (the gradient of the function it optimizes), that depends on the previous state \(x_k\) and data \(y\). Note that we need to use \(y\) in every step to actually optimize our function. Similarly we repeatedly inject the data \(\mathbf{e}\) in our set-up in every step of the recurrence. If \(\mathbf{e}\) was provided only at the start, e.g. via \(\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}\), then the iterative process would not be stable1, as its solution would depend only on its boundary conditions.

The structure of using several layers to embed input tokens into a hidden latent space is based on empirical results analyzing standard fixed-depth transformers (Skean et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Kaplan et al., 2024). This body of research shows that the initial and the end layers of LLMs are noticeably different, whereas middle layers are interchangeable and permutable. For example, Kaplan et al. (2024) show that within a few layers standard models already embed sub-word tokens into single concepts in latent space, on which the model then operates.

After

3.1. Macroscopic Design

The model suggests 3 new functional groups: prelude \(P\), the core recurrent block \(R\), and coda \(C\). While keeping the stucture primarily around decoder-only transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017; Radford et al., 2019). The core block is set between the prelude and coda blocks. And by looping the core we can put an indefinite amount of "verses".

The idea behind the 3 groups.

  • \(P\), the prelude, embeds the input data into a latent space using multiple transformer layers.
  • \(R\), the core recurrent block, is the central unit. It's responsible for recurrent computation modifying states \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\).
  • \(C\), the coda, has 2 main responsibilities. It un-embeds from latent space using several layers and contains the prediction head of the model.

Motivation for this Design.

The minimal setup required for learn stable iterative operators includes the following.

  • An initial starting state (a random starting point, \(s_0\)).
  • A previous state to build upon (\(s_{i-1}\)).
  • The input data (\(e\)) injected at every single step.
A good example is gradient descent of a function \(E(x, y)\), where \(x\) may be the variable of interest and \(y\) the data. Gradient descent on this function starts from an initial random state, here \(x_0\), and repeatedly applies a simple operation (the gradient of the function it optimizes), that depends on the previous state \(x_k\) and data \(y\). Note that we need to use \(y\) in every step to actually optimize our function.

The formal architecture.

Given a number of recurrent iterations \(r\), and a sequence of input tokens \(\mathbf{x} \in V^{n}\) these groups are used in the following way to produce output probabilities \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times |V|}\). As shown in Figure 2.

  • The prelude produces the embedded input data \(\mathbf{e} = P(\mathbf{x})\).
  • The initial random state \(s_0\) is drawn from some standard deviation \(\sigma\) distributed normally. \(\mathbf{s}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_{n \cdot h})\)
  • The core recurrent block repeatedly produces a new state \(s_i\) while still using the original embedded input data \(\mathbf{e}\). \(\mathbf{s}_i = R(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{s}_{i-1}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, \dots, r\}\).
  • The coda produces the final output probabilities for predicting the next token from the last state. \(\mathbf{p} = C(\mathbf{s}_r)\).

Notice we repeatedly inject the data \(\mathbf{e}\) in our set-up in every step of the recurrence. Similarly to what's mentioned in the motivation. If \(\mathbf{e}\) was provided only at the start, e.g. via \(\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}\), then the iterative process would not be stable1, as its solution would depend only on its boundary conditions.

This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs \(\mathbf{e}\) in every step (Bansal et al., 2022) and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization, i.e. path independence (Anil et al., 2022).

The inspiration for the architecture.

The structure of using several layers to embed input tokens into a hidden latent space is based on empirical results analyzing standard fixed-depth transformers (Skean et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Kaplan et al., 2024). This body of research shows that the initial and the end layers of LLMs are noticeably different, whereas middle layers are interchangeable and permutable. For example, Kaplan et al. (2024) show that within a few layers standard models already embed sub-word tokens into single concepts in latent space, on which the model then operates.

The general rule

The general rules I used in my writing were “known before new” (mention known concepts before introducing new ones), “anchor the reader before adding weight” (establish the main concept immediately, such as in the initial sentence or title), and “one core claim per paragraph”.
entry.summary: Rewriting the section 3.1 explaining the macro of the latent recurrent-depth model.
